objectives: Hear /p/ followed by /r/ at the beginning of a taught word.
Blend initial /pr/ without inserting an extra vowel.
Identify words beginning with pr and distinguish them from p-only words.
Listen through the whole word to confirm the blend.
concepts: A consonant blend contains adjacent consonant phonemes that remain audible.
The pr onset contains /p/ followed by /r/.
Smooth blending keeps the consonants close without adding a vowel.
Listening for /r/ distinguishes pr-words from words beginning with /p/ alone.

definitions.definition: Two adjacent consonant sounds that can both be heard, such as /p/ and /r/ in pram.
The initial consonant sound or group before the vowel.
Joining phonemes closely in order without inserting an extra vowel.

workedExamples.prompt: Say the first two sounds in pram.

workedExamples.solution: Keep /p/ and /r/ close and blend to read pram.
Pram begins with /p/ then /r/; Pam begins with /p/ and has no /r/ after it.

commonMistakes: Skipping /r/ and reading pram as Pam.
Treating pr as one phoneme instead of two.
Guessing from the first letter without listening for /r/.
keyTakeaways: Keep both consonants audible and close together.
Pram, press, print and prop begin with pr.
Check the whole word after blending.
revisionPoints: Do not insert a vowel between the consonants.
Contrast pram with Pam to hear the difference.

mixedReview.prompt: What is the best way to check a blend?
mixedReview.answer: Listen for both sounds in order

mixedReview.answer: Blend the rest of the word
